XVII.|OF THE APOSTLES.|343}}</noinclude>brethren sent away Paul, to goe vnto the sea: but Silas and Timothee remained there. {{verse|chapter=17|verse=15}}† And they that conducted Paul, brought him as farre as Athens, and receiuing commaundement of him to Silas and Timothee, that they should come to him very speedily, they departed.

{{verse|chapter=17|verse=16}}† And vvhen Paul expected them at Athens, his spirit vvas incensed vvithin him, seeing the citie giuen to Idolatrie. {{verse|chapter=17|verse=17}}† He disputed therfore in the synagogue vvith the Ievves, & them that serued God, and in the market-place, euery day vvith them that were there. {{verse|chapter=17|verse=18}}† And certaine Philosophers of the Epicures and the Stoikes disputed vvith him, and certaine said, Vvhat is it that this {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=∷ ''σπερμολόγος.''}}∷ vvord-sovver vvould say? But others, He seemeth to be a preacher of nevv {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=∷ ''dæmoniorum.''}}∷ gods. because he preached to them {{sc|Iesvs}} and the resurrection. {{verse|chapter=17|verse=19}}† And apprehending him, they led him to Areopagus, saying, May vve know vvhat this new doctrine is that thou speakest of? {{verse|chapter=17|verse=20}}† for thou bringest in certaine nevv things to our eares. Vve vvil know therfore vvhat these things may meane. {{verse|chapter=17|verse=21}}† ( And al the Athenians, and the strangers seiourning there, emploied them selues to nothing els but either to speake, or to heare some newes.) {{verse|chapter=17|verse=22}}† {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=∷ The Epistle for S. Dionysius Areopagita. Octob. 9.}}∷ But Paul standing in the middes of Areopagus, said:

Ye men of Athens, in al things I perceiue you as it vvere {{sup|‖}} superstitious. {{verse|chapter=17|verse=23}}† For passing by and seeing your {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=∷ The Aduersaries (in the nevv Test. 1580) translate, ''your deuotions'', most corruptly against the nature of the Greeke word ''(2 Thes. 2, 4'') and most wickedly, against the laudable deuotion of good Christians, calling the Pagans idolatrie and superstition, their deuotions.}}∷ {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=∷ ''τὰ σεβάσματα''}}∷ Idols, I found an altar also vvherevpon vvas vvritten, To the vnknowen God. That therfore vvhich you vvorshippe, not knovving it, the same do I preach to you. {{verse|chapter=17|verse=24}}† The God that made the vvorld and al things that are in it, he being Lord of heauen & earth, dvvelleth {{MarginNote|margin=left|margin-width=65|text=''Act. 7, 48.''}}* not in {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=∷ God is not concluded in Temples, nor needeth them for his necessitie of dvvelling, or other vses of indigence. See Annot. c. 7. Act. v. 48. · Act. 7, 48.}}∷ temples made vvith hand, {{verse|chapter=17|verse=25}}† neither is he serued vvith mens hands, needing any thing, vvhereas him self giueth life vnto al, and breathing, and al things: {{verse|chapter=17|verse=26}}† and he made of one al mankinde, to inhabite vpon the vvhole face of the earth, assigning set times, and the limits of their habitation, {{verse|chapter=17|verse=27}}† for to seeke God, if happily they may feele or finde him, although he be not farre from euery one of vs. {{verse|chapter=17|verse=28}}† For in him vve liue and moue and be, as certaine also of your ovvne poëtes said, {{MarginNote|margin=right|margin-width=65|text=∷ ''Aratus.''}}∷ ''For of his kinde also vve are''. {{verse|chapter=17|verse=29}}† Being therfore of Gods kinde, vve may not suppose, {{sup|‖}} the Diuinitie to be like vnto gold or siluer, or stone, the grauing of art and deuise of man. {{verse|chapter=17|verse=30}}† And the times truely of this ignorance vvhereas God dispised, novv he denounceth vnto men that al euery<noinclude>{{rh|||vvhere}}</noinclude>
